snippet.title: Their old mask was worth $4.6 Million!
snippet.description:
In a recent legal case, an elderly French couple lost their lawsuit against a second-hand dealer over a rare African mask found in their attic. The Ngil mask, crafted by the Fang people of Gabon, was sold to the dealer for €150 ($165) and later auctioned for €4.2 million ($4.6 million). The couple claimed that the dealer misled them about the mask's value, rejecting a €300,000 ($329,300) goodwill offer. However, the judge ruled in favor of the dealer, citing the couple's "inexcusable negligence and frivolity" for not researching the object's true worth before selling it. The mask, believed to be one of around 10 surviving examples globally, was controversially put up for sale, leading to protests by Gabonese community members who called for its repatriation. Despite the State of Gabon's efforts to cancel the sale, the court rejected the motion.

The legal dispute highlighted the complexities surrounding cultural heritage, as the mask was linked to the colonial era when French governor René-Victor Edward Maurice Fournier acquired it in 1917. The auction catalog provided vague details about the mask's provenance, acknowledging its collection in 1917 during Fournier's Gabon tour. Gabonese community members argued that such artifacts, looted during French colonization, should not be sold. The court's decision not to cancel the sale raised questions about the ethical considerations surrounding the spoliation of cultural works and the dignity of affected communities.

snippet.title: He found $12 Million worth of gold coins while doing plubing work!
snippet.description:
Dr. Jose Garcia, a country doctor from San Diego, Texas, quietly accumulated over 500 gold coins during the Great Depression. In response to Roosevelt's gold hoarding regulations, Garcia clandestinely buried his treasure beneath his home on St. Joseph Street, sharing the secret only with his daughter, Gloria, and her husband, Hector Lopez. When Dr Garcia died, Gloria and Hector made multiple attempts to find the coins but were unsuccessful. They believed their father had unearthed and sold them, and forgot about them.


However, decades later, in 2002, plumber Serafin Trevino stumbled upon Garcia's buried treasure while addressing plumbing issues at the property. His discovery ignited a legal dispute between Trevino and Garcia's descendants, ultimately leading to the rightful ownership of the coins by Gloria Garcia-Lopez and her husband. Despite the potential financial windfall, the Garcia-Lopez family's focus remained on community stewardship, as evidenced by their establishment of a foundation providing scholarships to first-generation Hispanic college students. The remaining coins found a home in the Museum of South Texas History, where they serve as a tangible link to the town's vibrant past, ensuring the legacy of "Dr. Garcia's Gold" endures for generations to come.
